content: Countries that still lack adequate immunization programs were visited for site assessments in 2–4 Member States annually between 2013 and 2015. Guidance and best practice documents were published by June 2014 to support these efforts. The application of the Guide to Tailoring Immunization Programmes (TIP) targets the general public, healthcare workers, and ministries of health. People choose not to vaccinate themselves or their children for various reasons, including complacency, lack of access, inconvenience, or lack of confidence in vaccines or the services providing them. In the diverse European Region, each country must have the capacity to diagnose these reasons accurately, design tailored responses, and adapt communication or service delivery to meet the needs of susceptible populations. Immunization programs should also define specific subpopulations and deliver campaigns and services tailored to their needs and preferences. To reduce vaccine refusals and encourage parents to vaccinate their children according to national immunization schedules, the Regional Office developed an innovative guide to help Member States tailor vaccination responses to the unique needs of targeted populations. The guide aims to increase demand for vaccination in vulnerable and underserved populations. Launched in April 2013, the TIP guide has been actively promoted and expanded across Member States. Its implementation is being assessed through qualitative methods, including online surveys, key informant interviews, and focus groups, to evaluate acceptance of TIP recommendations and the resources dedicated to their implementation. Milestones achieved include the rollout of TIP in two Member States annually (2013–2015), documentation of best practices by the end of 2014, and submission of two articles to peer-reviewed journals on TIP and its application (2014–2015). The quality of measles, rubella, and congenital rubella syndrome (CRS) surveillance must be high enough to detect sporadic cases and classify them as endemic or imported based on disease epidemiology and virus genotype. High-quality case-based surveillance requires the integration of clinical, epidemiological, and laboratory data using unique identifier numbers at every level. This information must be collected, analyzed, and communicated effectively and promptly to health workers and decision-makers to enable appropriate public health action. Surveillance systems for adverse events following immunization (AEFI) must also detect, monitor, and respond to suspected cases in a timely manner. Regular training and adequate information systems are critical components of this effort. Global experience in eradicating smallpox and poliomyelitis, as well as eliminating measles and rubella in the Americas, demonstrates the need for high-quality, case-based surveillance systems to detect and investigate suspected cases, provide timely responses, and document the absence of endemic cases. However, some Member States in the European Region still lack such systems. In 2012, 13 Member States failed to report case-based data for measles, and 25 did not report case-based data for rubella. Additionally, four countries lacked nationwide rubella surveillance systems. Improvements in rubella surveillance are needed by integrating national systems. The Regional Office is assisting countries in establishing and improving case-based surveillance systems through technical and capacity-building sessions, IT support, and securing political commitment. High-quality surveillance will simplify and improve reporting to the Regional Office, increasing the relevance and reliability of feedback to Member States. This feedback is provided through regional situation analyses, routine monthly reports, and direct communication with Member States. Collaboration with the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) aims to improve surveillance quality, increase data use in response activities, reduce reporting workload, and synchronize surveillance efforts. The WHO Measles and Rubella Laboratory Network (MR LabNet) focuses on increasing and maintaining laboratory capacity in countries, emphasizing prompt investigation of suspected cases and better availability of genetic data for analysis. Laboratories are encouraged to facilitate cross-border sample transport to address delays in testing. Integration of clinical, epidemiological, and laboratory data is essential for high-quality case-based surveillance. Member States using unique identifiers can integrate data more readily and will be targeted for initial integration efforts and technical assistance. Laboratory and epidemiological data submitted to the Regional Office are not always reconciled before dissemination, highlighting the need for improved data integration systems. Milestones include implementing systems to collect monthly case-based measles and rubella data at the regional level by the end of 2013, producing regular epidemiological and virological reports, and developing timelines for integrating rubella-related surveillance systems. Continued accreditation of at least 95% of national measles/rubella laboratories is expected annually (2013–2015). Vaccine safety concerns can significantly impact the acceptance of routine measles and rubella vaccines. Strengthening national capacity to manage immunization-associated risks is essential. This includes improving risk identification, assessment, and mitigation strategies, applying standardized procedures, and developing contingency plans. Regular assessment of injection practices is also necessary. A manual on vaccine safety and risk management has been developed, outlining recommended processes for addressing vaccine safety issues. Technical assistance and training sessions will support immunization programs and regulatory authorities in building risk management approaches and strengthening vaccine vigilance systems. Despite progress toward measles and rubella elimination, outbreaks continue in the Region. Between 2010 and 2012, over 100,000 measles cases were reported, with a peak of 37,073 cases in 2011. Outbreaks persist due to factors such as the accumulation of susceptible individuals, low vaccination coverage in certain groups, declining public acceptance of immunization, and health system reforms affecting immunization services. Member States must develop action plans for responding to measles or rubella outbreaks, including principles for large-scale response activities and long-term measures. Regional guidelines on outbreak response are being developed to assist Member States in creating comprehensive national response plans. An annually updated outbreak response plan will be required as part of the measles and rubella elimination verification process.
